analysis.one_liner: Requires data brokers to let people see, correct, and opt out of sale of their personal records.
analysis.headline: The bill, with five Senate sponsors, never left the Commerce Committee: it got no hearing, no vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Data brokers are companies that buy and sell personal information about people who are not their customers — where you live, what you buy, your income, your interests. This bill would have banned brokers from getting that information by lying about who they are, required them to keep accurate records, let people review their own file once a year for free, dispute errors, and opt out of marketing use. It also would have required data security programs, breach notifications, and an audit trail, with the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforcing the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal information is collected and sold without their knowledge. They would gain free annual access to what data brokers hold on them, a way to fix errors, a right to opt out of marketing use, and stronger protection against breaches.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose personal data is sold

how_it_helps.text: Bans data brokers from obtaining personal information through false statements or forged, stolen, or fraudulent documents.
Requires brokers to set up accuracy procedures, give individuals a free annual way to review their file, and correct disputed information after a written request.
Gives individuals a way to opt out of having their information used, shared, or sold for marketing purposes.
Requires a comprehensive data security program, individual notice of breaches or unauthorized access, and audit measures to trace access to personal data.
Makes violations enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general, who could sue for injunctions, restitution, and civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation.
Requires the FTC to set up a public website listing covered data brokers and explaining consumers' rights.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the marketing businesses built on their data, which would face compliance costs for accuracy reviews, consumer access, opt-outs, audits, and security programs — and would lose some sales of personal information.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on data brokers and would be passed at least partly to their business customers, and the bill relies on FTC rulemaking with broad authority to grant exceptions, so how much protection people actually get depends on agency rules not yet written.

The bill exempts brokers processing information about a company's own customers or employees, and lets brokers treat information covered by the Fair Credit Reporting Act as compliant under existing law, leaving part of the market under older, narrower rules.
It does not create a private right to sue for individuals; enforcement runs only through the FTC and state attorneys general, so enforcement depends on agency priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address real harms: inaccurate data broker files can affect whether someone gets a job, loan, or apartment, and breaches of broker-held data expose millions of people at once. The costs are compliance burdens on a profitable industry and some loss of data-marketing sales. The main weakness is design, not principle — broad FTC discretion to grant exceptions and no individual right to sue could narrow the promised protections considerably.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on September 14, 2017, joined by Sens. Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Franken, and Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation that same day.
No further action appears in the record: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the data-marketing industry, which kept operating with no accuracy, access, opt-out, or audit requirements, and buyers of personal data who faced no new rules.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were progressive Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican signed on, and a Republican-run committee never brought the bill up.

industries.note: The bill targeted the core of the data broker business model: it would have forced accuracy checks, free consumer access to files, marketing opt-outs, audits, and security programs, with FTC and state penalties. These companies profit by assembling and selling personal information about people who are not their customers, so consumer control directly cuts into what they can collect and sell.
Marketers buy data broker profiles to target advertising; the opt-out right would shrink the pool of sellable profiles and the accuracy requirements would raise the cost of the data they buy.

industries.industry: Banks, insurers, and employers using background screening
industries.note: These businesses buy broker data to evaluate applicants, so they would face higher data costs, but they would also benefit from more accurate records when making decisions about people.
